title: Serverless Computing
tagline: No servers to manage, no idle costs, infinite scale on demand — and the trade-offs every architect must understand before going serverless.

sections.content:
In 2014, AWS quietly launched a service called Lambda with a deceptively simple promise: upload a function, pay only when it runs. That single idea has since reshaped how millions of applications are architected. **Serverless computing** does not mean servers have disappeared — it means *you* never have to think about them. The cloud provider handles provisioning, patching, capacity planning, operating-system upgrades, and auto-scaling. You supply the business logic; the platform supplies everything else.

The term encompasses two closely related ideas. **Function as a Service (FaaS)** — AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, Azure Functions — is the purest form: a single handler function invoked on demand. **Backend as a Service (BaaS)** extends the idea to fully managed backends: Firebase, Supabase, Cognito, Auth0. In practice, when engineers say "we went serverless," they usually mean FaaS plus a constellation of managed services (databases, queues, storage) stitched together by event triggers.

Why does this matter? Traditional deployment forces a painful choice: provision enough servers to handle peak traffic (expensive idle capacity during quiet periods) or under-provision and risk outages during spikes. Serverless sidesteps the dilemma entirely. A function that handles one request per day and a function that handles one million requests per minute can use the exact same code, the same deployment model, and the same billing mechanism — both cost precisely what they consume.

This chapter builds a complete mental model of serverless: how function invocations work under the hood, why cold starts happen and how to fight them, how event-driven composition replaces monolithic servers, the economics that make serverless a win in some scenarios and a loss in others, and the architectural patterns that experienced serverless teams use in production. By the end, you will be able to decide — with numbers, not instinct — when to go serverless and when not to.

sections.title: Taxi vs Car Ownership vs a Bus Line
sections.content:
Running a **traditional server** is like owning a car. You pay insurance, maintenance, and registration every month whether you drive it or not. When ten friends need rides simultaneously, you're stuck — you only have one car. You chose the model, you pay for it around the clock.

**Serverless** is like Uber. You open the app only when you need a ride, pay only for the distance travelled, and Uber automatically dispatches as many cars as passengers request — whether that's two or two thousand. You never touch a steering wheel, never schedule an oil change. The catch: there is a **pickup wait** (the driver has to drive to you first — the serverless equivalent of a cold start). For a quick trip where you'd otherwise sit in traffic anyway, the wait barely matters. For an ambulance call, you cannot afford to wait — you need a dedicated vehicle on standby.

**Provisioned Concurrency** is the serverless equivalent of a car-service company that keeps a limousine idling outside your building. You pay a retainer whether it moves or not, but when you walk out, it's ready immediately — zero wait.

A **monolithic always-on server** is like a city bus: it runs on a fixed route and schedule, carries many passengers at once, and is economical only if the seats stay mostly full. If your traffic pattern is unpredictable or bursty, you're paying for empty seats all night.

sections.title: How Serverless Actually Works: The Container Lifecycle
sections.content:
When you deploy a Lambda function, you upload a deployment package (a ZIP of your code plus dependencies, or a container image). The package sits dormant in S3 or ECR until an event triggers it.

**Step 1 — Invocation**: An event source fires. API Gateway forwards an HTTP POST. An SQS message arrives. A scheduled EventBridge rule fires. Lambda receives the trigger payload.

**Step 2 — Container acquisition**: Lambda checks whether a warm container is available for this function. A **warm container** is an existing execution environment from a previous invocation that has not yet been recycled. If one is available, Lambda reuses it immediately — this path takes milliseconds. If no warm container exists (first invocation, or function hasn't been called in a while), Lambda must create a new one — the **cold start** path.

**Step 3 — Cold start (if needed)**: Lambda pulls the execution environment: sets up the micro-VM (using AWS Firecracker, a lightweight KVM-based hypervisor), loads the chosen runtime (Node.js 20, Python 3.12, Java 21, etc.), initialises the runtime, and runs your **initialisation code** — everything outside the `handler` function. This phase takes 100ms to 2 seconds depending on runtime and package size.

**Step 4 — Handler execution**: Lambda calls your `handler` function with the event payload and a context object. Your code runs, interacts with downstream services (DynamoDB, S3, external APIs), and returns a response. Execution time is billed in 1ms increments.

**Step 5 — Container freeze**: After the handler returns, Lambda freezes the container (pauses execution, reclaims CPU). The container stays warm for a period — typically several minutes — and will be reused for the next invocation, completely skipping steps 2 and 3. Eventually, if no invocations arrive, Lambda recycles the container entirely.

This lifecycle explains several important consequences. Initialisation code outside the handler runs once per cold start — put expensive setup there (SDK clients, database connections). The `/tmp` directory (512 MB) persists across warm invocations on the same container — useful for caching but not reliable as durable storage. Concurrency is handled by spinning up additional containers in parallel — not by a thread pool inside one container.

sections.title: Cold Starts: Root Causes, Measurement, and Mitigation
sections.content:
Cold starts are the most debated aspect of serverless. Understanding them precisely lets you decide when they matter and what to do about them.

**Why runtimes differ**: Java and .NET have large JVM/CLR startup times — cold starts can hit 1–3 seconds for a fat JAR. Node.js and Python have lightweight interpreters — cold starts are typically 100–300ms. Go compiles to a native binary with no interpreter overhead — cold starts are 50–100ms. AWS Lambda SnapStart (Java) partially mitigates this by snapshotting the initialised JVM state.

**Why package size matters**: Lambda downloads your deployment package from S3 before initialising. A 10 MB Node.js ZIP initialises much faster than a 250 MB ZIP with every npm package ever written. Tree-shaking, bundling with esbuild or webpack, and excluding dev dependencies are practical steps that reduce both cold start time and cost.

**VPC penalty**: When a Lambda function needs to access resources inside a private VPC (an RDS database, an ElastiCache cluster), Lambda must create an Elastic Network Interface (ENI) in your VPC subnets. Historically this added 10+ seconds to cold starts. AWS significantly improved this with the Hyperplane ENI sharing model (2019), reducing VPC cold start overhead to milliseconds — but the lesson remains: understand the network topology before assuming VPC Lambda is free.

**Provisioned Concurrency**: You can tell Lambda to keep N containers pre-initialised at all times. Those containers incur a per-second cost regardless of invocations, but every invocation hitting them is guaranteed a warm start. This is the correct solution for latency-sensitive APIs. You can combine it with Application Auto Scaling to ramp Provisioned Concurrency up before peak hours and down during off-peak, balancing cost and latency.

**Lambda SnapStart** (Java 11+): Lambda takes a snapshot of the fully initialised execution environment after the init phase. On cold start, rather than re-initialising from scratch, Lambda restores from the snapshot — reducing cold start by up to 90% for Java functions.

**Practical mitigation checklist**: (1) Use a lightweight runtime if latency is critical. (2) Bundle and tree-shake dependencies aggressively. (3) Move all initialisation outside the handler. (4) Enable Provisioned Concurrency for user-facing paths. (5) For Java, enable Lambda SnapStart. (6) Keep warm with a low-frequency scheduled ping only as a last resort (unreliable, wasteful).

sections.title: Event-Driven Architecture: The Composability Engine
sections.content:
The real power of serverless is not any single function — it is the ability to wire cloud services together into workflows using events as the connective tissue. This style is called **event-driven architecture (EDA)**.

Consider an e-commerce order pipeline: a customer submits an order → API Gateway invokes `createOrder` Lambda → Lambda writes to DynamoDB → DynamoDB Stream fires → `processOrder` Lambda reads the stream, deducts inventory, publishes an SQS message → `sendConfirmation` Lambda reads from SQS, renders an email template, and sends via SES → a second SQS consumer runs `notifyWarehouse` Lambda to create a fulfillment task. This entire pipeline handles arbitrary throughput, recovers from partial failures automatically (SQS retry with dead-letter queue), and costs nothing when no orders are being placed.

**Decoupling with queues**: Placing an SQS queue between producers and consumers is the single most impactful pattern in serverless architecture. The producer does not need to know who consumes the message; the consumer processes at its own pace; messages are durably stored if the consumer fails; retries are automatic; and the Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) catches poison-pill messages without blocking the pipeline.

**Fan-out with SNS + SQS**: Publish one event to an SNS topic; multiple SQS queues (and their Lambda consumers) subscribe. One order event simultaneously triggers inventory update, email notification, analytics ingestion, and fraud scoring — all in parallel, all decoupled, none aware of each other.

**Orchestration with Step Functions**: For complex workflows with branching, retries, timeouts, and human approval steps, AWS Step Functions provides a state machine that orchestrates Lambda functions without each function knowing about the next step. Step Functions logs every transition — invaluable for debugging multi-step workflows.

**EventBridge rules**: Route events from any source (your app, SaaS partners, AWS services) to any target (Lambda, SQS, Step Functions) based on JSON pattern matching. A single EventBridge bus can decouple dozens of microservices with zero code in the routing layer.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Several production-grade patterns are demonstrated here. SDK clients (`dynamo`, `sns`) are created outside the handler — they initialise once per cold start and are reused across warm invocations, avoiding repeated TLS handshakes and connection overhead. The `ConditionExpression: 'attribute_not_exists(orderId)'` on the DynamoDB write is an **idempotency guard** — if the same `orderId` is submitted twice (e.g. a network retry), DynamoDB rejects the duplicate rather than double-writing. Publishing to SNS rather than calling downstream services directly implements the **fan-out decoupling** pattern: the `createOrder` function doesn't need to know about email, warehouse, or analytics consumers.

sections.title: Serverless Economics: When It Saves Money, When It Doesn't
sections.content:
The pricing model of AWS Lambda has two components: **invocation count** and **compute duration**. As of 2024, Lambda charges $0.20 per million requests and $0.0000166667 per GB-second of compute (512 MB function running 100ms = 0.5 GB × 0.1s = 0.05 GB-seconds at $0.000000833 per invocation). The first 1 million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds per month are free forever.

**Scenario A — Low-traffic webhook**: 50,000 requests/month, 200ms average duration, 512 MB memory. Cost: ~$0 (entirely within free tier). The equivalent always-on `t3.micro` (1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM) costs $8.50/month. Serverless wins decisively.

**Scenario B — Spiky batch job**: A nightly report that runs 100,000 Lambda invocations at midnight and almost nothing during the day. Serverless cost: ~$0.02 in requests + a few cents in compute. An always-on server would sit idle 23 hours a day. Serverless wins.

**Scenario C — High-throughput API**: 10,000 requests/minute × 60 × 24 × 30 = 432 million requests/month. Lambda cost: $86 in requests + substantial compute cost (potentially hundreds of dollars depending on duration). Two `t3.large` instances (4 vCPU, 8 GB, load-balanced) cost ~$120/month and handle this volume comfortably. The gap widens at higher sustained throughput. Dedicated compute wins.

**Scenario D — Database-heavy functions**: Lambda adds function compute cost on top of DynamoDB/RDS costs. If most of your latency budget is database I/O, the function cost is relatively small — but you are still paying for both layers. A long-running DynamoDB stream processor that runs continuously may be cheaper on ECS Fargate.

The **break-even point** between Lambda and a dedicated EC2/Fargate instance is typically around 3–5 million requests per month at 100–200ms duration per invocation. Below that threshold, serverless almost always wins. Above it, model your specific traffic pattern.

**Memory sizing matters for cost**: Lambda allocates CPU proportionally to memory. Doubling memory from 512 MB to 1024 MB doubles the per-second cost but often halves execution time (CPU-bound functions), resulting in the same or lower total cost. Tools like AWS Lambda Power Tuning (open-source) automatically find the cost-optimal memory setting for any function.

sections.title: Statelessness: Constraints and Patterns
sections.content:
Lambda's stateless design is not a limitation to work around — it is an architectural principle that enables automatic horizontal scaling. Because each invocation is independent and no shared memory exists between invocations, Lambda can run 10,000 concurrent invocations without any container being aware of the others. No shared mutable state = no race conditions = no need for distributed locks in the function itself.

But applications need state. Here is how stateless functions handle common state patterns:

**Session state**: Store session tokens in DynamoDB or ElastiCache (Redis). Include the session token in every API call. The function fetches session state from the store on each invocation. Lambda's concurrency model means any container can handle any request — session affinity is neither possible nor desirable.

**Caching**: The `/tmp` directory (up to 10 GB since 2022) persists across warm invocations on the same container. You can cache slow-to-compute values (configuration, compiled templates, ML model weights) in `/tmp`. The caveat: you cannot control which container handles a request, so `/tmp` is a best-effort cache, not a reliable shared cache. For shared caching, use ElastiCache.

**Idempotency**: Because Lambda can retry on failure (SQS triggers retry if the handler throws; API Gateway does not retry, but clients do), your handlers should be **idempotent** — safe to invoke multiple times with the same input. The standard pattern: generate a unique key from the event payload, check DynamoDB for a previous result with that key, return the cached result if found, otherwise process and save. AWS offers the Lambda Powertools Idempotency utility (Python and Java) to handle this automatically.

**Transactions**: For multi-step operations that must be atomic, use DynamoDB transactions (`TransactWriteItems`), which atomically write up to 100 items across tables — all succeed or all fail. For cross-service transactions, AWS Step Functions with compensating transactions implements the Saga pattern without requiring distributed locks.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
# serverless.yml — Serverless Framework declarative configuration
# Defines Lambda functions, API Gateway routes, SQS triggers, and DynamoDB table

service: orders-api

provider:
  name: aws
  runtime: nodejs20.x
  region: us-east-1
  memorySize: 512          # MB — also controls CPU allocation
  timeout: 10              # seconds; max is 900 (15 min)
  logRetentionInDays: 14
  environment:
    ORDERS_TABLE: !Ref OrdersTable
    ORDER_EVENTS_TOPIC: !Ref OrderEventsTopic
  iam:
    role:
      statements:
        - Effect: Allow
          Action:
            - dynamodb:PutItem
            - dynamodb:GetItem
            - dynamodb:UpdateItem
            - dynamodb:Query
          Resource: !GetAtt OrdersTable.Arn
        - Effect: Allow
          Action: sns:Publish
          Resource: !Ref OrderEventsTopic

functions:
  createOrder:
    handler: src/orders/create.handler
    events:
      - httpApi:
          path: /orders
          method: POST
    # Uncomment to eliminate cold starts for this user-facing function:
    # provisionedConcurrency: 5

  processOrderQueue:
    handler: src/orders/process.handler
    reservedConcurrency: 50   # cap concurrency to protect downstream DB
    events:
      - sqs:
          arn: !GetAtt OrdersQueue.Arn
          batchSize: 10            # up to 10 messages per invocation
          functionResponseType: ReportBatchItemFailures  # partial batch success

  sendEmail:
    handler: src/notifications/email.handler
    events:
      - sqs:
          arn: !GetAtt EmailQueue.Arn
          batchSize: 1   # one email per invocation for clean error isolation

resources:
  Resources:
    OrdersTable:
      Type: AWS::DynamoDB::Table
      Properties:
        BillingMode: PAY_PER_REQUEST   # serverless billing for DB too
        AttributeDefinitions:
          - { AttributeName: orderId, AttributeType: S }
        KeySchema:
          - { AttributeName: orderId, KeyType: HASH }

    OrderEventsTopic:
      Type: AWS::SNS::Topic

    OrdersQueue:
      Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
      Properties:
        VisibilityTimeout: 60   # must be >= Lambda timeout
        RedrivePolicy:
          deadLetterTargetArn: !GetAtt OrdersDLQ.Arn
          maxReceiveCount: 3    # retry 3 times before DLQ

    OrdersDLQ:
      Type: AWS::SQS::Queue

    EmailQueue:
      Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
sections.explanation: Several production configuration patterns are present. `reservedConcurrency: 50` on the queue processor caps how many Lambda containers can run simultaneously — protecting a downstream database from being overwhelmed during a traffic spike. `functionResponseType: ReportBatchItemFailures` enables partial batch success: if a batch of 10 SQS messages has 1 failure, only the failed message is retried rather than the entire batch being requeued. `VisibilityTimeout` on SQS must be at least as long as the Lambda timeout to prevent a message becoming visible again while it is still being processed. The `RedrivePolicy` with `maxReceiveCount: 3` routes poison-pill messages to the DLQ after 3 failed attempts, preventing infinite retry loops from clogging the queue.

sections.title: Observability: The Hardest Part of Serverless
sections.content:
Debugging a traditional server application is familiar: SSH in, read logs, attach a debugger. In serverless, your application is distributed across hundreds of short-lived containers that you cannot SSH into, running in parallel across multiple availability zones, often involving five or more different AWS services. Observability is not optional — it is the only way to understand what is happening.

**Structured logging**: Always log JSON, never plain strings. AWS CloudWatch Logs ingests Lambda output automatically. Structured JSON lets you query logs with CloudWatch Insights using SQL-like syntax: `filter statusCode = 500 | stats count() by functionName`. Include `requestId`, `userId`, `orderId`, and `durationMs` in every log line. AWS Lambda Powertools (available in Python, TypeScript, Java) provides a structured logger that automatically includes Lambda context metadata.

**Distributed tracing with X-Ray**: AWS X-Ray instruments the entire invocation chain — API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB → SNS → downstream Lambda. Each segment shows latency, errors, and annotations. You can visualise the service map and identify which hop is causing latency. Instrumenting your handlers adds ~10 lines of code with Powertools' `Tracer`.

**Metrics and alarms**: Beyond default Lambda metrics (invocations, errors, duration, throttles, concurrent executions), emit **custom business metrics** using CloudWatch EMF (Embedded Metric Format) — a JSON log line that CloudWatch automatically turns into a metric. Alarm on `Errors / Invocations > 1%` and `p99 duration > 3000ms` for every production function.

**Dead Letter Queues as an observability tool**: A message in the DLQ is a signal that a failure occurred and was not self-healing. Alarm on DLQ depth > 0. Each DLQ message contains the original payload and error information — enough to replay or investigate without any logging.

**Chaos and limits awareness**: Lambda has account-level concurrency quotas (default 1000 concurrent executions per region). A burst of traffic can exhaust this quota and throttle all functions in the account. Monitor concurrent executions and request a limit increase proactively. `reservedConcurrency` on critical functions guarantees they always have capacity even when other functions are busy.

sections.title: Vendor Lock-In, Portability, and Alternatives
sections.content:
Serverless's greatest strength — deep integration with the cloud provider's ecosystem — is also its greatest strategic risk. A Lambda function wired to API Gateway, SQS, DynamoDB, SNS, EventBridge, and Cognito is not merely a technical artefact; it is a set of business commitments to AWS.

**The portability spectrum**: A pure computational function (input → output, no side effects) is trivially portable. A function that calls `DynamoDBClient`, reads from SQS via Lambda trigger conventions, and publishes to SNS requires significant rearchitecting to run on Google Cloud Run or Azure Container Apps. The trigger mechanism and SDK calls are all AWS-specific.

**Mitigation strategies**: (1) **Hexagonal architecture / ports and adapters**: isolate AWS-specific code in thin adapter layers; business logic only sees abstract interfaces. The handler becomes a thin adapter that translates AWS events into domain objects and calls domain services. (2) **Infrastructure-agnostic frameworks**: Serverless Framework, SST (Serverless Stack), and AWS CDK all generate CloudFormation, keeping infrastructure-as-code portable within AWS but not across clouds. (3) **OpenFaaS / Knative**: open-source FaaS platforms that run on Kubernetes, any cloud or on-premises. Function code is identical; the trigger mechanism is standardised.

**Alternatives to Lambda for long-running workloads**: AWS Fargate runs container tasks without managing EC2 instances — suitable for jobs that run 15 minutes to hours. AWS Batch optimises batch job scheduling across spot instances. AWS ECS with auto-scaling bridges the gap between serverless and traditional containers — still no server management, but persistent processes with warm state.

**The multi-cloud myth**: No meaningful production system runs Lambda functions on Azure. The operational tooling, IAM model, VPC integration, and service integrations are all cloud-specific. "Cloud-agnostic" is a planning fiction for most teams. Choosing a cloud provider is a long-term commitment; make it deliberately, not by accident.

sections.title: When to Use Serverless and When Not To
sections.content:
After understanding the mechanics, economics, and trade-offs, the decision framework becomes straightforward.

**Use serverless when**:
- **Traffic is bursty or unpredictable**: a marketing campaign that sends 10,000 requests in one hour then goes quiet is a perfect fit
- **Traffic is low and predictable**: a webhook receiving 500 events/day fits comfortably in Lambda's free tier
- **Event-driven processing**: image resizing on S3 upload, document indexing on database write, asynchronous email sending — all ideal
- **Scheduled jobs**: nightly reports, daily data syncs, hourly health checks — run without maintaining a cron server
- **Rapid prototyping**: Lambda + API Gateway + DynamoDB deploys a full API in minutes with zero infrastructure configuration
- **Microservices at small scale**: each domain (orders, payments, notifications) as its own Lambda function set with independent deployments

**Do not use serverless when**:
- **Sub-50ms P99 latency is required**: even with Provisioned Concurrency, cold starts can still occur during scaling events; dedicated servers with connection pooling and warm JIT are faster
- **Continuous workloads run 24/7**: a data pipeline ingesting 10,000 events/second around the clock costs more on Lambda than on two Fargate containers
- **Persistent connections are required**: Lambda cannot maintain WebSocket connections or persistent gRPC streams directly (API Gateway WebSocket API is a workaround with limitations)
- **Execution exceeds 15 minutes**: use Fargate, Batch, or ECS
- **High-memory or GPU workloads**: Lambda max is 10 GB RAM, no GPU support; use EC2 or SageMaker
- **Complex stateful workflows without Step Functions**: manually managing workflow state in Lambda handlers becomes a maintenance nightmare

**The honest answer for most teams**: a hybrid architecture wins. User-facing APIs on always-warm compute (ECS, App Runner, or Lambda with Provisioned Concurrency). Asynchronous processing (email, webhooks, ETL, notifications) on standard Lambda. Scheduled batch jobs on Lambda. Database-heavy analytics on Fargate or EMR. Serverless is a tool in the toolkit, not a religion.

**Historical context**: The serverless model was not invented by AWS. Hook.io (2013) offered hosted function execution before Lambda. Iron.io and PiCloud offered similar services. But it was AWS Lambda (November 2014) that mainstreamed the pattern, followed by Google Cloud Functions (2016) and Azure Functions (2016). The term 'serverless' itself is attributed to Ken Fromm in a 2012 blog post, though the modern FaaS model is what the term now universally refers to. Lambda's original use case at AWS was event processing for S3 — the HTTP use case via API Gateway came later.

**Common interview pitfalls and production mistakes**: (1) Initialising SDK clients inside the handler — this reconnects on every invocation, adding 50–200ms and risking connection exhaustion. Always initialise outside. (2) Setting SQS `VisibilityTimeout` shorter than Lambda `timeout` — messages become visible again while still being processed, causing duplicate processing. Rule: `VisibilityTimeout >= 6 × LambdaTimeout`. (3) Treating Lambda concurrency as a thread pool — concurrency means parallel containers, each single-threaded; do not share mutable state across invocations. (4) Missing DLQ configuration — without a DLQ, failed async invocations are silently dropped after retries. (5) Not modelling the break-even point before committing — run the numbers with your actual traffic pattern, not gut feel.

items: **Serverless/FaaS** means the cloud provider manages all infrastructure — provisioning, scaling, patching, and HA — you supply only the handler function and pay per invocation.

**Cold starts** occur when no warm container exists for a function; root causes include runtime choice, package size, and VPC ENI setup. Provisioned Concurrency eliminates cold starts at a fixed cost.

**Initialise expensive resources** (SDK clients, DB connections, config) outside the handler — they run once per cold start and are reused across warm invocations, dramatically reducing per-invocation latency.

**Event-driven composition** via SQS/SNS fan-out, DynamoDB Streams, and EventBridge lets you wire cloud services into scalable pipelines without any function needing to know about the others — decoupling is the core superpower of serverless.

**Economics are not always in serverless's favour**: serverless wins at low or bursty traffic; sustained high-throughput workloads often cost more than dedicated compute. Model your traffic pattern before deciding.

**Statelessness is a feature, not a bug**: it enables automatic horizontal scaling with zero coordination overhead. Manage session state externally (DynamoDB, Redis), use idempotency guards for safe retries, and use DynamoDB transactions for atomic multi-item writes.

**Observability requires active design**: use structured JSON logging, X-Ray distributed tracing, CloudWatch custom metrics, and DLQ alarms — distributed short-lived functions are impossible to debug without them.

quiz.question: What does 'serverless' actually mean in the context of AWS Lambda?
options: The code runs without any underlying hardware
Servers exist but are fully managed by the cloud provider — you do not provision or maintain them
The application has no server-side code, only a frontend
Functions are executed directly in the user's browser
quiz.explanation: Serverless does not mean no servers exist — it means you don't manage them. AWS provisions, scales, patches, and retires the containers that run your Lambda functions automatically, using lightweight Firecracker micro-VMs under the hood.

quiz.question: Which of the following correctly explains why initialising an SDK client OUTSIDE the Lambda handler improves performance?
options: Code outside the handler runs in a separate high-priority thread
Code outside the handler runs once per container cold start and is reused across warm invocations, avoiding repeated TLS handshakes and connection setup
AWS SDK clients cannot be instantiated inside async functions
Placing clients outside the handler enables Lambda to pre-load them from a global cache
quiz.explanation: Lambda containers are reused across warm invocations. Code outside the handler (the init phase) runs only once per cold start. On subsequent warm invocations, the already-initialised client is available immediately — saving the 50–200ms cost of reconnection and TLS negotiation on every call.

quiz.question: A Lambda function processing SQS messages has a timeout of 30 seconds. What should the SQS queue's VisibilityTimeout be set to, at minimum?
options: 30 seconds — matching the Lambda timeout exactly
60 seconds — double the Lambda timeout
180 seconds — at least 6 times the Lambda timeout
10 seconds — shorter than the Lambda timeout to allow fast retries
quiz.explanation: AWS recommends VisibilityTimeout >= 6 × Lambda timeout. If VisibilityTimeout is shorter than the Lambda execution time, the message becomes visible again before processing completes, causing another consumer to pick it up — resulting in duplicate processing. With a 30s Lambda timeout, set VisibilityTimeout to at least 180s.

quiz.question: What is a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) and why is it essential in serverless architectures?
options: A queue that stores responses from Lambda for later retrieval
An SQS queue that captures messages which failed processing after the maximum number of retries, preventing silent data loss
A priority queue that routes high-importance messages to dedicated Lambda containers
A DynamoDB table that logs Lambda execution errors for auditing
quiz.explanation: Without a DLQ, messages that fail processing after all retries are silently dropped. A DLQ captures these poison-pill messages so they can be inspected, debugged, and replayed. Alarming on DLQ depth > 0 is a critical production observability pattern — it signals a systematic failure that requires investigation.

quiz.question: Provisioned Concurrency in AWS Lambda is best described as:
options: A limit on the maximum number of simultaneous Lambda invocations to control costs
Pre-initialised containers kept warm at all times to eliminate cold starts, at a fixed hourly cost
Dedicated EC2 instances provisioned exclusively for a single Lambda function
A feature that enables Lambda to connect to resources inside a private VPC
quiz.explanation: Provisioned Concurrency keeps a specified number of Lambda execution environments fully initialised and ready to handle requests. Every invocation routed to a provisioned container has zero cold start latency. You pay for the provisioned capacity by the second regardless of whether invocations occur — trading cost for guaranteed low latency.

quiz.question: An e-commerce platform uses SNS + multiple SQS queues for order processing. What architectural benefit does this 'fan-out' pattern provide?
options: It guarantees exactly-once delivery of every order event
It allows multiple independent consumers (email, warehouse, analytics) to react to the same event without any consumer knowing about the others
It reduces DynamoDB costs by batching writes across consumers
It enables Lambda functions to share in-memory state across invocations
quiz.explanation: SNS fan-out decouples producers from consumers. Publishing one event to SNS delivers it to all subscribed SQS queues in parallel. Adding a new consumer (e.g. a fraud detection service) requires no changes to the producer or existing consumers — just subscribe a new SQS queue to the topic. This is the core composability superpower of event-driven serverless architecture.

quiz.question: A Lambda function processing 432 million requests per month at 200ms average duration with 512MB memory. Approximately how does this compare in cost to two t3.large EC2 instances?
options: Lambda is always cheaper due to pay-per-invocation pricing
Lambda costs significantly more than the EC2 instances at this sustained high throughput
They cost approximately the same — Lambda's free tier offsets the difference
Lambda is cheaper because 512MB memory functions have a heavily discounted rate
quiz.explanation: 432 million requests/month × $0.20/million = $86 in request charges alone, plus significant compute cost (432M × 0.2s × 0.5GB × $0.0000166667/GB-s ≈ $720). Two t3.large instances with a load balancer cost roughly $130-200/month and handle this traffic comfortably. Sustained high-throughput workloads almost always cost more on Lambda than dedicated compute.

quiz.question: Which of the following workloads is the WORST fit for AWS Lambda?
options: A nightly batch job that runs for 12 minutes processing 50,000 records
A webhook endpoint receiving approximately 500 events per day
A real-time financial trading system requiring sub-10ms P99 response latency
An image resizing service triggered by S3 file uploads
quiz.explanation: Lambda cold starts (100ms–2s) and the inherent overhead of container-based invocation make it incompatible with sub-10ms P99 latency requirements. Even with Provisioned Concurrency, Lambda adds overhead versus a dedicated in-process server. Real-time latency-critical systems need always-warm, pre-JIT-compiled processes with persistent connections — characteristics Lambda cannot guarantee.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of a `ConditionExpression: 'attribute_not_exists(orderId)'` in a DynamoDB PutItem call within a Lambda handler?
options: It speeds up the DynamoDB write by skipping the index update
It ensures the write is idempotent — rejecting duplicate writes if the same orderId is submitted more than once
It triggers a DynamoDB Stream event only on new item creation
It validates that the orderId attribute conforms to the expected data type
quiz.explanation: Lambda SQS triggers can retry failed invocations, and clients may retry failed HTTP requests — both can submit the same payload multiple times. A ConditionExpression that fails if orderId already exists turns the write into an idempotent operation: the first write succeeds, all subsequent duplicates are rejected with ConditionalCheckFailedException, which the handler catches and returns 409 Conflict. This prevents double-processing without requiring a separate deduplication lookup.

quiz.question: Why does Java have significantly longer Lambda cold starts than Node.js or Go?
options: Java functions are downloaded from a different S3 region, adding network latency
The JVM must initialise its bytecode interpreter and JIT compiler, load the classpath, and run static initialisers — a much heavier startup sequence than Node.js or a Go native binary
AWS allocates fewer CPU credits to Java Lambda functions during cold start
Java's garbage collector runs a full collection cycle before the handler can start
quiz.explanation: Node.js starts a lightweight V8 JavaScript engine; Go compiles to a native binary with no runtime interpreter overhead — both start in tens of milliseconds. Java requires initialising the JVM (class loading, bytecode verification, JIT compilation warm-up, static initialiser execution) which can take 500ms–2s for a typical Spring Boot or AWS SDK-heavy application. AWS Lambda SnapStart mitigates this by restoring from a pre-initialised JVM snapshot rather than initialising from scratch.
